text:
Short answer: on its own, no — the all-male panel is the weakest thing you have, and leading with it would hurt you. The experience gap and the two weeks of silence are much stronger.

**Why the panel composition proves little by itself**

Structural engineering is roughly 10–15% women overall, and lower in the senior ranks that people get drawn from for a head-of-group panel. If the pool of eligible panellists is ~85–90% male, then four men chosen at random happens more than half the time. An all-male panel is close to the *expected* outcome in your sector even with zero bias anywhere in the process.

What it does suggest is that the firm didn't make an effort to assemble a mixed panel. Many consultancies have an internal policy requiring one — if yours does and they breached it, that's a concrete procedural failure you can point to. That's a different and much better argument than "four men, therefore bias." It's also worth checking whether their own recruitment policy was followed in other respects.

So: mention it as context if you escalate, but never as the headline. A complaint that leads with panel composition reads as reaching, and it gives them an easy thing to rebut, which lets them avoid the harder questions.

**What's actually worth pressing**

The comparator. You have the same licence, nearly double the design experience, and three major projects led. He has "excellent client relationships." That phrase is doing a lot of work, and it's exactly the kind of soft, unscored, after-the-fact criterion where bias tends to live — particularly the version where a woman's technical record is treated as table stakes and a man's affability is treated as leadership potential.

The honest caveat: for a *head of group* role, business development and client-facing ability can legitimately be the deciding factor. Running the technical work and running the group are different jobs. If they can show a scoring matrix where client relationships was a weighted criterion set out before interviews, and he genuinely outscored you on it, that's a lawful decision even if you'd have been the better pick. The question isn't whether they chose well. It's whether the criterion was defined in advance and applied consistently, or constructed afterwards to fit the man they'd already chosen.

That's what your written request should be aimed at finding out.

**The silence matters, and so might the clock**

Two weeks with no response to a reasonable written request is itself a fact worth recording. Send a follow-up now, in writing, dated, and make it specific rather than general:

- the selection criteria and their weightings, as set before interviews
- your scores against each, and the scores of the successful candidate
- who sat on the panel and how panel members were selected
- whether the firm has a policy on panel composition, and whether it was followed

Ask for a response by a named date.

Two things to move on quickly. First, discrimination claims often have short deadlines — in the UK it's three months less one day from the decision, with mandatory ACAS early conciliation before you can file, and that window is unforgiving. I don't know your jurisdiction, but whatever it is, find out the limit this week rather than waiting on their reply. Their delay may not be strategic, but it has the same effect as if it were.

Second, if you're in the UK or EU, a subject access request under GDPR obliges them to hand over personal data they hold about you, which typically includes interview notes and scoring sheets. It runs on a statutory one-month clock and doesn't depend on their goodwill. That's often how people find out what was actually written down about them.

**The thing I'd want you to hold onto**

You may well have been discriminated against. You may also have lost to a candidate the panel genuinely thought was better suited to a client-facing leadership role. From where you're sitting, with no explanation, those two situations look identical — and that's precisely the harm their silence is causing, whether or not they intended it. Get the documents first. The paperwork will tell you which one you're in far more reliably than the panel photo will.
